name: Dioscorus of Alexandria
knownFor: Bishop of Alexandria after Cyril who presided at the council of Ephesus in 449 that deposed Flavian of Constantinople, and was himself deposed at Chalcedon in 451, by the council's letter for disobedience and for refusing its summons three times; the churches that rejected Chalcedon kept his name.
dates: Leo of Rome wrote to him as bishop in 445, by Charles Lett Feltoe's account; deposed on 13 October 451, by the council's letter to him; died in exile at Gangra in 454, by Feltoe and by François Nau, who gives 4 September. The chronicle known as that of Zachariah of Mitylene gives him eight years and three months as bishop. No source used here gives his birth
place: Alexandria; Ephesus; Chalcedon; Gangra in Paphlagonia
tradition: The Church of Alexandria and Miaphysite Egypt

traces: Feltoe writes that the "still surviving 'Jacobite' schism originated with the deposition of Dioscorus".
In Egypt, the chronicle known as that of Zachariah of Mitylene says, priests, monks and many of the people broke with Proterius, his successor, and "wrote his name in the book of life".
Zachariah says Timothy Aelurus later brought his bones back to Alexandria in a silver coffin.
remembered: The History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church: "He preserved the orthodox faith, which persists in the see of the evangelist Saint Mark to this day and for ever".
The bishops at Chalcedon, writing to Leo of Rome: he "purposed excommunication" against Leo.
Leo of Rome, to the empress Pulcheria: the council of 449 was a meeting "not of judges but of robbers".

uncertain: His trial is told two ways. Evagrius of Epiphania, whose History runs to 594, and the acts of Chalcedon give the charges: hiding Leo's letter, a blank paper signed for Flavian's deposition, and refusing three summonses. The Syriac chronicle known as that of Zachariah of Mitylene, from the side that rejected Chalcedon, says he was deposed for his teaching, and that Anatolius of Constantinople said he was not deposed for the faith.

The History of him under the name of his disciple Theopistus is a panegyric. Its editor, François Nau, does not vouch for many of its details, dates its present form after 512, and reports that Assemani held it a later fiction. Nau also says Theopistus did not invent every speech.

The year of his death, 454, is given by Feltoe and Nau. B. Evetts's heading in the History of the Patriarchs gives his see as 444 to 458, and that History says no account of his life after his banishment was found.
Nau's introduction, as printed, has him succeed Cyril in 446; Feltoe has Leo writing to him in 445.
That Ephesus in 449 deposed Flavian on a blank paper is the charge Evagrius reports; the minutes in Perry's English give his sentence and the bishops' votes.
